title: MongoDB Documents: BSON, _id, Size Limits & Data Modeling
summary: A deep tour of the MongoDB document itself — how BSON encodes every type on the wire, what the _id field guarantees, why 16 MB is a hard ceiling, and how to choose between embedding and referencing. Covers internals, practical patterns, trade-offs, and the mistakes that bite in production.

chapters.title: What a Document Actually Is
points: A document is an ordered set of field/value pairs — MongoDB's unit of storage, roughly analogous to a row, but self-describing and nested.
Documents live in collections; collections live in databases. No schema is enforced by default, so two documents in one collection may have completely different fields.
Field order is preserved in BSON and returned in insertion order — unlike a JSON object in most languages, where key order is not guaranteed.
Example: { _id: 1, name: "Ada", langs: ["js", "go"], addr: { city: "Dublin" } } — scalars, arrays, and subdocuments in one record.
Documents are self-describing: every field name is stored in every document, so short field names save real disk and RAM.
Field names cannot be empty in most contexts, and field names starting with $ or containing . were historically illegal (allowed since MongoDB 5.0 but still risky in query and update expressions).
Duplicate field names are technically representable in BSON but not created by drivers; the server rejects most of them.
Documents are atomic: a single-document write (insert, update, delete) is always all-or-nothing, even across nested arrays.
Maximum nesting depth is 100 levels — exceeding it errors out with 'BSONObj exceeded maximum nested object depth'.
A collection stores documents with no fixed column set; adding a field is a per-document act, not a table migration.
Optional schema validation ($jsonSchema with validator) reintroduces enforcement when you want it, with validationLevel strict|moderate and validationAction error|warn.
The document model's key promise: data that is accessed together is stored together, so one disk read can serve a whole entity.
Contrast with SQL: a customer + orders + line items is 3 tables and 2 joins relationally, or 1 document with 1 read in MongoDB.

chapters.title: BSON: The Binary Encoding
points: BSON = Binary JSON: a binary-serialized document format that is the actual on-disk and on-the-wire representation. JSON is only the display layer.
Wire layout: int32 total length | element list | 0x00 terminator. Each element is: 1-byte type code | cstring field name | value.
BSON is length-prefixed, which makes it traversable — a parser can skip a subdocument by reading its length rather than scanning for a closing brace.
BSON is designed to be lightweight (little overhead), traversable (fast skipping), and efficient (C-friendly fixed-width numeric types).
BSON adds types JSON lacks: ObjectId, Date, Binary, Decimal128, Regex, Timestamp, MinKey/MaxKey, and distinct int32/int64/double.
BSON is bigger than JSON for some data (length prefixes, type bytes) and smaller for others (numbers stored as fixed-width binary, not decimal text).
Extended JSON (canonical vs relaxed) is the lossless text form: {"n": {"$numberLong": "42"}} in canonical, {"n": 42} in relaxed. mongoexport uses it.
Integers are little-endian; strings are UTF-8 with an int32 byte-length prefix and a trailing null.
Type codes to know: 0x01 double, 0x02 string, 0x03 embedded doc, 0x04 array, 0x07 ObjectId, 0x08 bool, 0x09 UTC datetime, 0x10 int32, 0x12 int64, 0x13 decimal128.
Arrays are encoded as documents with stringified numeric keys: ["a","b"] is stored as {"0":"a","1":"b"} — which is why huge arrays are costly.
Because array indices are stored as string keys, a 1-million-element array pays index-string overhead per element.
Practical consequence: renaming a long field across millions of documents can shrink a collection measurably.
bsonsize / Object.bsonsize(doc) in mongosh returns a document's exact encoded byte count — use it before you hit the limit.

chapters.title: The BSON Type Zoo
points: Double (1): 64-bit IEEE 754 float, the default numeric type from the shell and from JavaScript drivers.
String (2): UTF-8 only; invalid UTF-8 is rejected or replaced. Length is in bytes, not characters.
Object (3) and Array (4): nested documents and lists, arbitrarily deep up to the 100-level cap.
BinData (5): raw bytes with a subtype byte — 0x00 generic, 0x04 UUID, 0x07 compressed time series. Store hashes, thumbnails, encrypted blobs here.
ObjectId (7): 12 bytes, the default _id type. Covered in depth next chapter.
Boolean (8), Null (10), and Undefined (6, deprecated — drivers convert to null).
Date (9): signed 64-bit milliseconds since the Unix epoch, UTC only. No timezone is stored — the client must apply one.
Regex (11): pattern plus flags; used by $regex queries and stored regexes.
Int32 (16) and Int64 (18): exact integers. NumberInt(5) / NumberLong("5") in mongosh force them.
Decimal128 (19): 128-bit IEEE 754-2008 decimal, 34 significant digits — the only correct type for money. NumberDecimal("9.99").
Timestamp (17): an internal replication type (seconds + ordinal). Do not use it for application timestamps — use Date.
MinKey (-1) and MaxKey (127): sort sentinels that compare below and above every other type.
Type-bracketed comparison order (low to high): MinKey < Null < Numbers < String < Object < Array < BinData < ObjectId < Boolean < Date < Timestamp < Regex < MaxKey.
All numeric types compare and sort together: NumberInt(5), 5.0, and NumberDecimal("5") all match a query for 5.
$type queries by BSON type: db.c.find({ qty: { $type: "int" } }) or by numeric code; $type: "number" matches all numeric types.

chapters.title: The _id Field
points: Every document must have an _id. If you omit it, the driver (usually) or the server generates an ObjectId before insert.
_id is the primary key: it is unique within a collection and backed by a mandatory unique index named _id_ that cannot be dropped.
_id is immutable — you cannot $set it. Changing an identity means delete + reinsert.
_id can be any BSON type except an array. Arrays are banned because a multikey _id index would break uniqueness semantics.
_id may be a subdocument, but then field order matters for equality: { a:1, b:2 } and { b:2, a:1 } are different _id values.
Custom _id is a real optimization: use a natural key (email, SKU, ISO date bucket) and you get a free unique constraint and skip a second index.
In sharded collections the _id index stays unique only if _id is the shard key or a prefix of it — otherwise uniqueness is only per-shard.
_id is always returned by find() unless explicitly suppressed: find({}, { _id: 0, name: 1 }).
Insert with a duplicate _id raises E11000 duplicate key error — often the intended idempotency mechanism for retried writes.
Upserts use _id from the filter when possible: updateOne({ _id: k }, { $set: {...} }, { upsert: true }) is the idiomatic 'insert or merge'.
The _id index is used to route single-document reads and to feed the oplog, which identifies every affected document by _id.
Common mistake: using a monotonically increasing _id as the shard key, which hot-spots all inserts on one shard. Use hashed sharding or a compound key instead.

chapters.title: ObjectId Internals
points: An ObjectId is exactly 12 bytes, rendered as a 24-character hex string: ObjectId("65f1a3b4c2d1e0f9a8b7c6d5").
Layout: 4-byte big-endian seconds-since-epoch timestamp | 5-byte random value per process | 3-byte incrementing counter starting at a random value.
The old 3-byte machine ID + 2-byte process ID layout was replaced by the 5-byte random value in MongoDB 3.4 drivers — do not parse it for host info.
Because the timestamp leads, ObjectIds are roughly monotonically increasing, so _id sort approximates creation-time sort at second granularity.
getTimestamp() extracts the creation Date — so a separate createdAt field is often redundant for second-level precision.
Range-query by creation time by constructing a boundary ObjectId from a timestamp: ObjectId.createFromTime(date) as the lower bound.
Generated client-side by the driver, not the server — so an insert needs no round trip to learn its own id, and ids stay unique across many clients.
Uniqueness is probabilistic but strong: same second + same 5-byte random + counter collision is required for a clash.
12 bytes beats a 36-character UUID string (36 bytes) — but a UUID stored as BinData subtype 4 is 16 bytes and unordered.
Ordered ObjectIds mean new inserts land at the right edge of the B-tree — great for write locality, bad as a shard key.
Leaking ObjectIds in URLs leaks approximate creation times and rough record counts via the counter — use an opaque public id if that matters.
In mongosh, ObjectId() with no args mints a new one; ObjectId("...") parses. A 24-hex string in a query will NOT match an ObjectId — types must match exactly.

chapters.title: The 16 MB Document Size Limit
points: A single BSON document may not exceed 16 MiB (16,777,216 bytes) — a hard server limit, not a tunable.
The size is the encoded BSON size, including every field name, type byte, and length prefix — not the JSON text size.
Why the limit exists: it bounds per-document RAM use, prevents one document from monopolizing bandwidth, and keeps working-set behavior predictable.
The limit applies to documents at rest AND to intermediate aggregation results, replace documents, and the result of an update.
Object.bsonsize(db.c.findOne({_id: x})) tells you a document's true byte size before you push it further.
Growth-over-time is the usual failure mode: an unbounded array (comments, events, log lines) creeps toward the ceiling and then writes start failing.
The error surfaces as 'BSONObjectTooLarge' or 'Resulting document after update is larger than 16777216'.
Aggregation pipeline stages are also capped at 16 MB per output document — $group with $push on a high-cardinality key blows up the same way.
The pipeline's total memory per stage is capped at 100 MB by default; use allowDiskUse:true for large $sort / $group, which is a separate limit from the 16 MB doc cap.
GridFS is the escape hatch for large binaries: it splits a file into 255 KB chunks across fs.chunks with metadata in fs.files.
Better than GridFS for most media: store the blob in object storage (S3, GCS) and keep only the URL, size, and checksum in the document.
The bucket pattern caps growth: one document per (device, hour) holding at most N readings, with a count field so you can roll to a new bucket.
Rule of thumb: if a document routinely exceeds a few hundred KB, the data model is probably wrong, long before 16 MB becomes the wall.

chapters.title: Embedding: One Document, One Read
points: Embedding means nesting related data directly inside the parent document as a subdocument or array of subdocuments.
Example: an order document with an embedded items array — one find() returns the entire order, no join.
Query nested fields with dot notation: find({ "addr.city": "Dublin" }); index them the same way: createIndex({ "addr.city": 1 }).
Match a whole subdocument by equality and field order matters: find({ addr: { city: "Dublin", zip: "D2" } }) requires an exact structural match.
$elemMatch requires one array element to satisfy all conditions: find({ scores: { $elemMatch: { s: { $gt: 80 }, subj: "math" } } }) — without it, conditions can match different elements.
Update array elements with the positional operator $ (first match), $[] (all elements), or a filtered positional $[tag] with arrayFilters.
Array update operators: $push, $pull, $addToSet, $pop, and $push with $each/$slice/$sort to keep a capped, sorted top-N list.
Indexes on array fields are multikey: one index entry per element. A multikey index cannot also be a shard key and only one array field may be multikey per compound index.
Embed when: the relation is one-to-few, the child has no independent lifecycle, and you always read the child with the parent.
Embedding buys atomicity for free — a single-document update over parent and children is transactional with no session or transaction API needed.
Cost of embedding: duplicated data if the child is shared, larger documents (more I/O per read), and the size-limit risk from unbounded growth.
Watch document-growth churn: repeatedly growing a document forces WiredTiger to rewrite the whole record, so append-heavy embedded arrays cost write amplification.
Projection tames big embedded arrays: { items: { $slice: 10 } } returns only the first 10 elements.

chapters.title: Referencing: Linking Documents
points: Referencing stores a pointer — usually the related document's _id — instead of the data itself, and resolves it with a second query or a $lookup.
Manual reference: { authorId: ObjectId("...") } — the normal, recommended form. Your application knows the target collection.
DBRef: { $ref: "authors", $id: ObjectId("..."), $db: "blog" } — self-describing but not resolved by the server; drivers must dereference. Rarely worth it.
$lookup performs a left outer join inside an aggregation pipeline: { $lookup: { from: "authors", localField: "authorId", foreignField: "_id", as: "author" } }.
$lookup output is always an array; follow with $unwind (with preserveNullAndEmptyArrays for a true left join) to flatten it.
Index the foreignField — an unindexed $lookup does a collection scan per input document and turns into an O(n·m) disaster.
$lookup with a let/pipeline subform supports correlated joins and extra filtering on the joined side.
$graphLookup walks recursive references (org charts, category trees, follower graphs) with maxDepth and depthField.
Reference when: the relation is one-to-many with an unbounded many side, the child is large, or the child is shared and must stay consistent in one place.
Referencing costs a round trip (or a join stage) and gives up cross-document atomicity unless you open a multi-document transaction.
Child-to-parent references scale better than parent-holding-an-array-of-children: the array is the thing that grows without bound.
Two-way references (parent stores child ids AND child stores parent id) speed both directions but must be kept in sync — a classic drift bug.
Multi-document transactions exist (session.withTransaction) but cost performance and have a 60-second default runtime limit — treat them as the exception, not the design.

chapters.title: Choosing a Model: Trade-offs & Patterns
points: The governing rule: data that is accessed together should be stored together. Model for your queries, not for your entities.
One-to-few (a user's 3 addresses): embed. One-to-many (a post's comments, bounded): embed with a cap or bucket. One-to-squillions (log lines): reference from the child.
Many-to-many: store an array of ids on one or both sides, or use a dedicated join collection when the relationship itself has attributes.
Comparison row — read cost: embed = 1 read; reference = 2 reads or 1 aggregation with $lookup.
Comparison row — write cost: embed = 1 atomic write; reference = 2 writes needing a transaction for consistency.
Comparison row — duplication: embed duplicates shared data; reference stores it once.
Comparison row — growth risk: embed is bounded by 16 MB; reference is effectively unbounded.
Extended reference pattern: copy the few hot fields (author name, avatar) into the child alongside the id, so the common read needs no join.
Subset pattern: embed the top 10 reviews in the product document and keep the full set in a separate collection for the 'see all' page.
Computed pattern: store commentCount / totalPrice on the parent and maintain it with $inc, instead of recomputing an aggregate on every read.
Bucket pattern: group time-series readings into per-hour documents to cut document count and index size dramatically.
Outlier pattern: handle the 0.1% of documents that would blow the size limit (a celebrity with 10M followers) with an overflow flag and a spill collection.
Schema versioning pattern: keep a schemaVersion field so old and new document shapes can coexist during a rolling migration.
Duplication is acceptable when the copied data rarely changes; the cost of a join on every read usually exceeds the cost of an occasional fan-out update.

chapters.title: Gotchas, Pitfalls & Recap
points: Type mismatch silently returns nothing: find({ _id: "65f1..." }) will not match ObjectId("65f1..."). Always cast on the way in.
Storing money as a double loses precision: 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3. Use NumberDecimal or integer minor units (cents).
The shell defaults every bare number to double — NumberInt / NumberLong are required if the stored type matters to a consumer.
Dates have no timezone. Store UTC Date, render in the user's zone at the edge; never store a local-time string for sorting.
Unbounded arrays are the number one document-model failure — every embedded array needs an answer to 'how big can this get?'.
Long field names cost bytes in every document; 'transactionIdentifier' vs 'txId' across 100M documents is gigabytes of difference.
null and 'missing' are different at query time: { x: null } matches both missing and null; use { x: { $exists: true, $eq: null } } to distinguish them.
Comparing across types follows the BSON type order, so a query for { age: { $gt: 30 } } will never match age stored as the string "31".
Field names with dots or dollar signs are legal since MongoDB 5.0 but still break dot-notation queries and many update operators — avoid them.
Deep nesting hurts: past 3-4 levels, queries get unreadable and positional updates get painful, long before the 100-level cap.
DBRef adds indirection without server support — prefer manual references in almost every case.
$lookup on an unindexed foreign field is the most common cause of a slow aggregation; check with explain("executionStats").
Recap: BSON is the binary, typed, length-prefixed reality behind the JSON you see.
Recap: _id is the mandatory, immutable, uniquely indexed primary key — and ObjectId is a 12-byte, time-ordered, client-generated default you can replace with a natural key.
Recap: 16 MB is a hard ceiling that punishes unbounded growth; bucket, subset, or offload to object storage before you approach it.
Recap: embed for locality and atomicity, reference for unbounded or shared data, and let your query patterns — not entity diagrams — decide.
